Archive item 1: Maintenance Manual 2024
Source format: Maintenance Manual

1.1 This manual applies to all buildings, grounds, and fixed equipment owned or leased by Loxwood & District Sports Club, including the clubhouse, changing rooms, plant room, courts, croquet lawn, main gate, floodlighting masts, and irrigation system.

1.2 The Facilities Manager (FM) is responsible for the implementation of this manual. The Groundsman reports to the FM for all grounds-related tasks. The Club Steward is responsible for reporting defects found during daily opening checks.

1.3 Contractors engaged to carry out work on club premises must be made aware of the relevant sections of this manual before starting work. The FM must approve any deviation from these procedures in writing.

1.4 Routine tasks are recorded in the weekly log kept in the plant room. Exception reports are recorded in the same log but flagged with an ‘E’ prefix. The FM reviews the log every Friday.

---

**Section 2 – Routine Checks – Daily**

2.1 Clubhouse Entrance and Main Gate

- Check the main gate operates freely and the latch engages fully. If the gate swings back on its own, report to the FM. Do not oil the hinges without approval; the current hinges are sealed units and oiling attracts dust.
- Inspect the door closer on the clubhouse main entrance. It should close the door from a 30-degree opening in no more than 5 seconds. If it slams or fails to close, adjust the valve screw no more than half a turn. If the fault persists, log it as a defect.

2.2 Changing Rooms

- Check for leaks under the sinks and around the toilet bases. Wipe down any standing water. Note the condition of the sealant around the shower trays; report any dark spots or lifting edges.
- Verify that the hand dryer in the ladies’ changing room runs for at least 30 seconds. The timer is set at the factory and should not be adjusted without the FM’s say-so.

2.3 Boiler Room

Maintenance Manual 2024 governing revision date 2024-03-15 date. Record status: superseded.

- Read the pressure gauge on the main boiler (TC1). Normal operating pressure is 1.5 bar when the system is cold. If the reading is below 1.0 bar, top up the system using the filling loop. Record the topping-up in the log. If the reading is above 2.5 bar, do not touch anything; call the FM immediately.
- Check the boiler condensate trap for blockages. The trap is the clear plastic U-bend on the left side of the unit. If it is dry or full of debris, flush it with clean water.

2.4 Courts and Croquet Lawn

- Walk the perimeter of the tennis courts. Remove any debris that could damage the surface. Check the nets for sagging; the centre strap should be taut but not pulling the net down more than 5 cm.
- Inspect the croquet lawn for rabbit scrapes or worm casts. Lightly brush any casts flat with the back of a rake. Do not use a roller on the lawn during wet weather.

---

**Section 3 – Routine Checks – Weekly**

3.1 Floodlights

- Inspect the floodlight masts (M1, M2, M3) for obvious damage or loose fixings. Use binoculars from the ground; do not climb the masts unless trained and authorised.
- Test the floodlighting circuit using the test switch in the plant room. The test switch is labelled ‘FL TEST’. Run the lights for five minutes. Check that all lamps illuminate and that there is no excessive flicker. Record the test in the weekly log.
- Check the photocell on top of the clubhouse. It should be clean and free of cobwebs. If the lights are coming on during the day, clean the photocell lens with a soft cloth and check the time-delay setting.

3.2 Irrigation System

- Open the isolation valve for the irrigation system (valve V-4, located in the green cabinet by the croquet lawn). Check the pressure at the gauge. The reading should be between 2 and 3 bar. If the pressure is low, check the filter basket for debris.
- Run each irrigation zone manually for two minutes. The zone controller is in the same cabinet. Note any sprinkler heads that are not popping up fully or that are spraying unevenly. Clean the affected heads with a small brush. Do not adjust the arc on the heads; the arcs are set for each zone and adjusting them will cause dry patches.

3.3 Guttering and Downpipes
**Section 3 – Routine Checks – Weekly (cont.)**

3.3 Guttering and Downpipes

- After heavy rain, walk the full perimeter of the clubhouse and check that all gutters are running freely. Pay particular attention to the section above the kitchen, where leaves from the sycamore by the car park tend to collect.
- Clear any blockages you can reach safely from a ladder. Do not use a pressure washer on the gutters; it can force water back under the felt. If a blockage is above the flat roof over the store room, do not attempt to clear it yourself. Log it for the contractor.
- Check the downpipe outlets at ground level. The two outlets behind the bin store are prone to silting up. If water is pooling there, clear the silt with a trowel and flush the pipe with a bucket of clean water.
- Inspect the clip fixings on the downpipe run along the west wall. One clip was replaced in March 2024; the others are original. If any clip is loose, tighten it, but do not overtighten as the pipe is uPVC and can crack.

3.4 Boiler House – Additional Weekly Checks

- Check the boiler pressure again at the same time each week, preferably a Monday morning before the building is in use. Record the reading in the weekly log even if it is normal.
- Inspect the condensate trap again. If the trap has discharged debris twice in the same month, note this in the log and flag it for the annual service.
- Check the area around the boiler for any signs of water on the floor. A small amount of condensation on the pipes is normal in cold weather, but a puddle on the floor is not. If you find a puddle, dry it, check the source, and report it even if you cannot find a leak.
- Wipe down the exterior of the boiler casing with a dry cloth. Do not use any cleaning products on the controls.

3.5 Fire Alarm Call Points and Emergency Lighting

- Test one fire alarm call point per week, rotating through the building so that each call point is tested at least once per quarter. The call points are numbered on the inside of the cover: CP1 (reception), CP2 (main hall), CP3 (kitchen), CP4 (store room), CP5 (ladies’ changing room), CP6 (men’s changing room), CP7 (plant room).
- To test, insert the test key, wait for the alarm to sound, then reset using the panel in reception. The panel will show which call point was activated. Record the call point number and the date in the fire log.
- Check that the alarm sounder is audible in all areas, including the store room with the door closed. If it is not audible, report it immediately.
- Walk the building and check that all emergency lighting units are lit. The units in the main hall and the corridor should be checked with the mains supply on and again with the supply isolated using the test switch on the distribution board in the plant room. Leave the supply isolated for the full duration of the test (one hour) and check that the units remain lit for that period.
- Do not test the emergency lighting in the kitchen while the kitchen is in use. If the kitchen is occupied, defer the test and note the deferral in the log.

3.6 First Aid Kits

- Check the contents of the two first aid kits (reception and kitchen) against the contents list fixed to the inside of the lid. Replace any item that is missing or past its expiry date.
- Restock from the supplies cupboard. The cupboard is locked; the key is on the same ring as the plant room key. Order replacements for anything you use from the usual supplier.
- Check the eye wash bottles. The bottles have a four-month shelf life once opened; write the opening date on the bottle with the marker kept in the cupboard. If a bottle has no date or the date is more than four months old, replace it.
- Report any use of the first aid kit in the accident book, even if the injury was minor and no first aider was called.

3.7 Defibrillator

- Check the defibrillator unit on the wall outside the main hall. The green light on the front should be flashing steadily. If the light is not flashing, or is flashing red, report it to the FM immediately.
- Check the expiry date on the pads. The pads expire in May 2025. Do not open the sealed pouch to check the pads themselves; the pouch is only to be opened when the unit is used.
- Check that the sign above the unit is still in place and legible.
- Do not move the unit or store anything in front of it. The area must be kept clear at all times.

Archive item 2: Maintenance Manual 2026
Source format: Maintenance Manual

1.1 Purpose
This manual sets out the routine maintenance requirements and operating procedures for the Club’s buildings, plant, and grounds. It is intended for use by Facilities staff, the Club’s named contractors, and duty managers. Where a procedure in this manual differs from a manufacturer’s instruction, the manufacturer’s instruction shall take precedence unless a deviation is recorded in the Site Exception Log (Appendix C) and approved by the Facilities Manager.

1.2 Scope
The manual covers the main clubhouse, the two squash courts, the fitness suite, the changing rooms, the bar and kitchen plant, the boiler room, the swimming pool plant room, the outdoor courts, the bowling green, and the car park. It does not cover tenanted areas or the private flats above the north wing.

1.3 How to Use This Manual
Each section contains a description of the plant or area, the routine task schedule, and the specific tolerances or settings that must be maintained. All staff and contractors must familiarise themselves with the sections relevant to their work before starting any task. If a conflict is found between this manual and any site notice, the manual governs unless the notice is dated after the manual’s revision date and is signed by the Facilities Manager.

1.4 Definitions
- PPM: Planned Preventive Maintenance.
- TC1 / TC2 / TC3: Test certificates or test checkpoints as referenced in the relevant section.
- Duty Manager: The senior staff member on site outside normal office hours.
- Facilities Manager: The named individual responsible for the upkeep of the Club’s premises and plant.

2. General Responsibilities

2.1 Facilities Staff
The Facilities staff are responsible for carrying out the weekly and monthly checks listed in this manual, recording results in the appropriate log books, and reporting any defect to the Facilities Manager within 24 hours. Any defect that presents an immediate danger to persons or property must be reported immediately and, if necessary, the plant isolated.

2.2 Contractors
All contractors must be from the approved list in Section 9. They must sign in and out at the main office, and they must be accompanied by a member of Facilities staff when working in the plant rooms or on the roof. Contractors must provide their own risk assessments and method statements for any task that is not covered by a standing risk assessment held in the office.

Maintenance Manual 2026 governing revision date 2026-01-10 date. Record status: current.

2.3 Duty Managers
Duty managers are responsible for the first-line response to any plant alarm or failure outside office hours. They must be familiar with the emergency isolation points listed in Section 8 and must contact the on-call Facilities person as per the rota held in the office. Duty managers must not attempt repairs beyond the scope of their training.

3. Boiler Room

3.1 Plant Description
The boiler room contains two condensing gas boilers (B1 and B2), each rated at 120 kW, serving the underfloor heating in the main hall and the domestic hot water calorifier. The boilers are linked by a common flow header. A single flue serves both boilers.

3.2 Routine Checks – Weekly
- Check boiler pressure gauges: should read between 1.0 and 1.5 bar when cold.
- Check for any visible water leaks around pumps and valves.
- Record gas meter reading in the boiler log book.
- Check condensate trap is clear and draining.

3.3 Routine Checks – Monthly
- Check burner flame appearance via the sight glass (should be blue and stable).
- Check flue gas temperature; record in log.
- Test the low water cut-off on B1 per the manufacturer’s instructions.
- Check the expansion vessel pre-charge pressure (should be 1.0 bar).

3.4 Boiler Control Settings
The following control settings are current as of the revision date of this manual. These settings were updated following the winter 2025 performance review and are to be used for the 2026 heating season.

| Parameter | Setting |
|-----------|---------|
| Flow temperature setpoint (B1) | 75°C |
| Flow temperature setpoint (B2) | 70°C |
| Return temperature setpoint | 55°C |
| Weather compensation curve | 20°C at 0°C outside, 65°C at -5°C outside |
| Night set-back time | 22:00 to 05:30 |
| Frost protection on | 5°C flow temperature |
- Check the level of the top dressing. Use the depth gauge stored in the plant room. The dressing should be between 25 mm and 35 mm deep across the whole court. Record readings at the four corners and the centre in the court log book.
- Check the line markings. The lines should be clearly visible. If they are fading, arrange for re-marking as per Section 4.2.6.
- Check the perimeter edging. The edging must be flush with the surface. If the edging is proud, it can catch the ball or cause a trip hazard. Report any proud edging to the Facilities Manager.
- Check the drainage outlets at the low side of the court. Clear any silt or debris from the outlet grilles.

4.2.4 Seasonal Maintenance

Spring (April)

- After the winter, carry out a full depth check as per Section 4.2.3.
- Top up the surface where the depth is below 25 mm. Use kiln-dried sand and brick dust mix (60/40 by volume). The mix is stored in the shed behind the pavilion. Do not use builders sand.
- Roll the court with the roller stored in the shed. Roll in two directions, at right angles to each other. Do not roll when the surface is wet.
- Brush the court after rolling to redistribute the dressing.

Autumn (October)

- Carry out a final depth check before the winter.
- Top up the surface as required.
- Check the court is free from moss or algae growth. If moss is present, treat with the algicide approved by the Facilities Manager. Apply per the manufacturer's instructions and keep the court off limits for 48 hours.

Winter

- Do not brush the court when it is frozen.
- If the court is waterlogged, do not play on it. Use the squeegee to remove standing water. Do not walk on the court more than necessary when it is waterlogged.
- Check the court weekly for frost heave. If the surface has lifted, do not roll it. Report to the Facilities Manager.

4.2.5 Repairs

- Small holes or divots: fill with the top dressing mix and firm down with the back of a rake. Water lightly if the mix is dry.
- Larger damaged areas (greater than 0.5 m²): contact the court surface contractor. The current contractor is CourtCraft Surfaces Ltd. Their contact details are on the noticeboard in the plant room. Do not attempt to repair large areas with top dressing alone.
- Line markings: re-marking should be carried out by the contractor. Do not use household paint. The correct paint is a water-based acrylic line paint, colour white.

4.2.6 Record Keeping

All checks and maintenance tasks for TC1 must be recorded in the court log book, which is kept in the plant room. Each entry must include the date, the name of the person carrying out the task, and any readings taken. If a fault is found, record what was done about it, or if it was reported, to whom and when. The log book is reviewed by the Facilities Manager on the first Monday of each month.

4.3 Macadam Court – TC2

Tennis Court 1 surface type artificial clay type. Record status: current.

4.3.1 General Principles

The macadam court is a bound surface. It is less delicate than the artificial clay court but still requires regular care. The main risks are weed growth at the edges, moss in shaded areas, and the surface becoming slippery if algae builds up.

4.3.2 Weekly Checks

- Sweep the court with the yard brush to remove loose grit and debris.
- Check the surface for cracks. Small hairline cracks can be left, but any crack wider than 5 mm should be reported.
- Check the net posts and winders as per Section 4.2.2.

4.3.3 Monthly Checks

- Check for weed growth along the perimeter and at the base of the net posts. Remove weeds by hand or with a scraper. Do not use a strimmer on the court surface.
- Check the surface for moss or algae. If present, treat with the same algicide used on TC1.
- Check the line markings. Macadam court lines are painted and will fade over time. Arrange re-marking as required.

4.3.4 Seasonal Maintenance

Spring

- Sweep the court thoroughly.
- Check for any frost damage. The surface may have cracked if water has got into it and frozen. Report any significant cracking to the Facilities Manager.
- Treat any moss or algae as per Section 4.3.3.

Autumn

- Clear fallen leaves promptly. Do not allow leaves to build up as they can stain the surface and make it slippery.
- Check the court is draining properly. Standing water should clear within 30 minutes of rain stopping. If water pools for longer, check the falls and report.

Winter
4.3.5 Re-marking of Line Markings

All line markings on TC2 are painted with acrylic court-marking paint. The current colour for all lines on the macadam court is white. This is to match the colour used on Tennis Court 1 and to keep a uniform appearance across the club. Tennis Court 1 line color white color. Record status: current. The paint is supplied by CourtCare Ltd, order code ACW-5L. The Facilities Manager holds the account details. Do not substitute with another brand or type of paint unless authorised in writing. Substitute paints may not adhere correctly to the macadam surface and could cause slipping.

4.3.5.1 When to Re-mark

The lines should be re-marked when they become faded or when the surface has been repaired. As a guide, check the lines at the monthly inspection. If the white paint no longer contrasts clearly with the surrounding surface when viewed from the net, arrange for re-marking. In practice, this is usually every 12 to 18 months depending on usage and weather. Courts used for matches may need more frequent attention.

4.3.5.2 Preparation

Before any painting is done, the court must be clean and dry. Follow this sequence:

1. Sweep the court thoroughly with the yard brush. Pay particular attention to the lines. Remove all loose grit and debris.
2. If there is any moss or algae on the surface, treat it as per Section 4.3.3 and allow it to dry completely before proceeding.
3. Wash the area to be painted with clean water and a stiff brush if there is any ingrained dirt. Allow the surface to dry fully. Painting onto a damp surface will cause the paint to peel.
4. Mask off the lines with 50 mm low-tack tape. Use a tape measure and string line to ensure the lines are straight and at the correct width. The tape should be laid just outside the line edge so that the finished line is the correct width.
5. Protect any adjacent areas, such as the net posts, with polythene sheeting if there is a risk of paint splatter.

4.3.5.3 Painting Procedure

- Use a medium-pile roller for the main body of the line. Cut in the edges with a small brush where needed.
- Apply the paint in one even coat. Do not over-roll. Two thin coats are better than one thick coat. Allow the first coat to dry for at least 2 hours before applying the second coat if required.
- Keep a wet edge when rolling to avoid lap marks.
- Remove the tape while the paint is still slightly wet. If the tape is left until the paint is fully dry, it may pull the paint off the surface.

4.3.5.4 Drying and Reinstatement

The paint will be touch-dry in about 1 hour, but the court should not be used for at least 24 hours after painting. Put up the "Court Closed" signs and remove the nets. The court can be reopened once the paint is fully cured and the Facilities Manager has inspected the work. Record the date of re-marking in the court log book.

4.3.5.5 Line Widths and Measurements

All lines are 50 mm wide unless stated otherwise. The dimensions for the singles and doubles courts are given in the diagram in Appendix A. When re-marking, do not rely on the old lines as a guide if the surface has been repaired. Measure from the net posts and the court edges using the measurements in the appendix. If in doubt, contact the Facilities Manager before starting.

4.3.5.6 Paint Storage and Disposal

Store paint tins in the plant room on the metal shelving, away from direct heat and frost. Keep the lids firmly closed when not in use. Do not store paint on its side. Empty tins and used rollers should be disposed of in the general waste. Do not pour paint or wash water down the drains. Wash brushes and rollers in the sink in the plant room using cold water. The wash water can be poured onto the gravel area behind the plant room.

4.3.6 Court Repairs

Small repairs to the macadam surface can be carried out by the grounds staff. Larger repairs must be reported to the Facilities Manager who will arrange for a contractor.

4.3.6.1 Hairline Cracks

Hairline cracks, up to 3 mm wide, can be left. They do not usually worsen quickly and the surface remains playable. Monitor them at the monthly check.
The edges of the court, especially along the fence line and around the gate, can crumble with age. If the edge has broken away by more than 50 mm, the court is losing its shape and the base may be exposed. Small edge damage can be repaired with the cold-lay mix, but do not build the new edge up in one thick layer. Build it up in thin layers, letting each layer go off before adding the next. If the edge damage runs for more than 2 m in one stretch, report it to the Facilities Manager. A contractor will need to cut a clean edge and relay the section.

4.3.6.5 Weed Growth

Weeds growing through the macadam, or in the joint between the court and the kerb, should be treated with the weedkiller kept in the locked cabinet in the plant room. Apply on a dry day when no wind is forecast. Do not spray on the planted borders. Pull out any large weeds by hand first. Treated areas should be kept clear of play for 24 hours. If weeds keep coming back in the same spot, check whether the surface has broken up underneath. Report any persistent problem to the Facilities Manager.

4.3.6.6 Moss and Algae

Moss and algae can make the court slippery, particularly on the shaded side near the trees. At the monthly check, look for green or black patches. Treat with the algicide and moss killer from the plant room, following the dilution rates on the label. Apply on a dry day. Do not walk on the court until the treatment has dried. If the court is regularly slippery, the Facilities Manager should be told. It may be that the surface needs a deeper clean with the pressure washer, or that the shade is keeping the court damp and the trees need pruning.

4.3.6.7 Lifting or Blistering

If the surface lifts or blisters, this is usually a sign of moisture trapped under the macadam. Do not break the blister. Mark the area and report it to the Facilities Manager immediately. Do not attempt a repair. The affected area will need to be cut out and relaid by a contractor. Blistering is often caused by the court being sealed with an impermeable coating when the base was still damp. Any future sealing work must only be carried out in dry weather.

4.3.7 Hard Court Surface Type and Use

Tennis Court 2 surface type hard type. Record status: current. This is a macadam court, and it is to be maintained as such. The maintenance schedule in this manual applies to all hard courts on the site, including Tennis Court 1 and Tennis Court 2, unless a specific court is named.

Hard courts are for tennis and netball only. Do not allow bikes, scooters, or skateboards on the surface. Do not drag chairs, tables, or other equipment across the court. When the clubhouse furniture is moved for events, use the plywood sheets stored behind the plant room to protect the surface. The plywood sheets are heavy and should be carried by two people.

4.3.7.1 Acceptable Use

Hard courts may be used for tennis coaching, club play, and social events arranged by the committee. The court may also be used for netball by the local league team, subject to the booking arrangements in the clubhouse. No other ball games are permitted. Do not use the court for badminton or for any activity that involves dragging equipment. Do not set up marquees or heavy staging on the court without the prior written permission of the Facilities Manager.

4.3.7.2 Cleaning

The court should be swept at least once a week, more often in autumn when leaves are falling. Use the wide yard brush from the plant room. Do not use a metal rake on the surface. Remove chewing gum and other sticky marks with a scraper, taking care not to gouge the surface. The court should be jet washed once a year, in the spring, using the pressure washer. Hold the lance at a shallow angle and keep the nozzle moving. Do not use a rotary brush attachment. Do not jet wash within 48 hours of a frost forecast, and do not jet wash if the court has been painted in the last month.

4.3.7.3 Winter Care

In freezing weather, do not attempt to remove ice with salt or a metal spade. Salt can damage the macadam and the surrounding grass. Spread the fine grit from the bin by the gate for grip, and leave the ice to thaw naturally. Do not play on the court when it is icy or when frost is on the surface. Play on a frozen court can damage the binder and cause the surface to crack. If the court has been flooded, do not play on it until the water has drained away completely. Standing water should drain within a few hours. If it does not, check the drainage channels around the court and clear any blockages.

Section 4.4 – Croquet Lawn

4.4.1 General Description

The croquet lawn is the level grass area to the south of the clubhouse, bounded by the yew hedge on the west, the hard court on the north, and the rose bed on the east. It is used for croquet from April to September and for occasional club social events outside that season. The lawn is a single playing surface and should be treated as such: the whole area, including the margins inside the boundary string, is part of the playing surface.

The lawn was re-turfed in 2021 and the drainage was renewed at the same time. The soil is a sandy loam over a gravel drainage layer. The lawn is maintained as a fine turf sward. It is not a general recreation area and must not be used for football, cricket, or any other ball game. Children must not play on the lawn unless they are taking part in a supervised croquet session.

4.4.2 Mowing

Croquet Lawn mowing height 12 mm. Record status: current. This is the current setting and must be maintained throughout the playing season. The height is measured from the bedknife to the sole of the mower and should be checked with a feeler gauge at the start of each week.

The lawn should be mown twice a week during the growing season (generally April to October) and once a week during the winter, weather permitting. Do not mow when the grass is wet or when frost is on the ground. Do not mow during or immediately after heavy rain. If the grass is very long because of a period of absence, do not cut more than one third of the leaf length in a single pass. Raise the bedknife for the first pass and then lower it to 12 mm for the second pass.

Use the Toro pedestrian mower kept in the plant room. The mower is set up for the croquet lawn and must not be used on the verges or the orchard. The verges are cut with the ride-on mower. The mower blades should be sharpened at least once a month during the playing season. Dull blades tear the grass and leave a white tip that is visible on the playing surface.

Mowing pattern: alternate the direction of mowing each time. Mow north-south one week and east-west the next. This prevents the grass from lying over in one direction. Do not mow in the same line every time, as this creates a stripe that is visible from the clubhouse and can also cause the grass to wear along the wheel marks.

Do not use a roller on the lawn. The surface should be kept firm but not artificially flattened. If the lawn becomes uneven, see Section 4.4.6 on levelling.

4.4.3 Irrigation

The lawn should be watered during dry spells. The aim is to keep the grass green and growing, not to flood the surface. Water in the early morning, before 8 am, or in the evening after 6 pm. Do not water in the middle of the day, as the water evaporates and the grass can be scorched.

Use the sprinkler on a stand, positioned at the edge of the lawn and moved around so that the whole surface receives water. Do not leave the sprinkler in one position for more than 20 minutes. The lawn should not be watered so heavily that water runs off the surface or pools. If water pools, the drainage is not working and the matter should be reported to the Facilities Manager.

During a hosepipe ban, the lawn may be watered using the water butt by the plant room, but only for the croquet lawn. The water butt is filled from the roof of the plant room. Do not use mains water for the verges or the flower beds during a ban.

4.4.4 Feeding and Top Dressing
The main pest affecting the croquet lawn is leatherjackets. Leatherjackets are the larvae of the crane fly. They feed on the roots of the grass and cause brown patches. If leatherjackets are suspected, lift a small square of turf and inspect the soil. The larvae are grey-brown and about 25 mm long. If leatherjackets are present, treat the lawn with a nematode application. The nematodes are purchased from the supplier on the contact list. The nematodes must be applied in the evening, when the soil is moist. Do not apply nematodes in bright sunlight.

Ants nests can also be a problem. If ants nests appear, they should be brushed flat with a stiff broom. Do not use ant powder on the lawn, as it will damage the grass. If the ants nests are persistent, contact the Facilities Manager.

4.4.9 Winter Maintenance

During the winter months, the croquet lawn should be rested. From the end of November to the end of February, the lawn should not be played on. The hoops should be removed and stored in the box in the plant room. The box is labelled "Croquet Hoops". The hoops should be cleaned and dried before storage.

The lawn should be kept clear of leaves and debris. Use the leaf blower kept in the plant room. Do not use the leaf blower on the verges, as it is set up for the croquet lawn. The leaf blower should be used on a low setting to avoid damaging the grass.

If the lawn becomes waterlogged during the winter, do not walk on it. Walking on a waterlogged lawn will damage the roots and leave permanent marks. If the lawn is waterlogged, report the matter to the Facilities Manager.

In February, the lawn should be scarified. Scarification removes the thatch and moss from the surface. Use the scarifier kept in the plant room. The scarifier is the machine with the wire tines. Set the scarifier to a depth of 3 mm. Do not scarify too deeply, as this will damage the roots. Scarify in one direction only, then collect the debris with a rake.

4.4.10 Renovation

A full renovation of the croquet lawn should be carried out every three to five years. The renovation is usually carried out in early September, after the main playing season. The renovation involves the following steps:

1. Mow the lawn at a low height, reducing the height gradually over a period of two weeks. Do not cut more than one third of the leaf length in a single pass.
2. Scarify the lawn to remove thatch and moss.
3. Aerate the lawn using the hollow tine aerator.
4. Top dress the lawn with a 50/50 mix of sand and loam.
5. Overseed the lawn with a fine fescue seed mix. The seed mix is kept in the plant room, in the bag marked "Croquet Lawn Seed".
6. Apply a spring/summer feed.
7. Water the lawn regularly for the first two weeks after renovation.

Do not allow play on the lawn for at least six weeks after renovation. The lawn should be kept moist during this period. If the weather is dry, water the lawn daily in the early morning.

4.5 Clubhouse Boiler

The Clubhouse Boiler provides heating and hot water for the clubhouse. The boiler is located in the plant room, in the corner nearest the rear wall. The boiler is a wall-mounted condensing boiler. Clubhouse Boiler boiler model Baxi 800 model. Record status: current. This is the current model and is the model that all replacement parts and servicing instructions in this manual refer to. If a different boiler is ever installed, this section must be updated and the Facilities Manager must be informed.

4.5.1 Safety Warnings

Before carrying out any work on the boiler, read the safety warnings in this section. Failure to follow the safety warnings may result in serious injury or death.

The boiler must only be serviced by a Gas Safe registered engineer. Do not attempt to service the boiler yourself unless you are Gas Safe registered. The boiler is a gas appliance and must not be tampered with by unqualified personnel.

Isolate the boiler from the gas supply and the electricity supply before carrying out any work. The gas isolation valve is located on the gas pipe, approximately 300 mm from the boiler.
4.6 Main Gate and Access Control

4.6.1 Overview

The Main Gate is the principal vehicle and pedestrian entrance to the club grounds, located on the east boundary adjacent to the clubhouse car park. It provides controlled access for members, staff, contractors, and visitors. The gate and its associated access control equipment are the responsibility of the Facilities Manager. Any fault or suspected fault with the gate or its locking mechanism must be reported to the Facilities Manager immediately. Do not attempt to force the gate open or closed if it is stuck or behaving erratically.

4.6.2 Gate Lock Type

Main Gate gate lock type electronic keypad type. Record status: current. This is the current type and is the type that all servicing and replacement instructions in this manual refer to. The electronic keypad is mounted on the pedestrian side of the gate, on the right-hand post, at a height of approximately 1.4 m from the ground. The keypad controls the electric strike on the pedestrian gate. The vehicle gate is operated by a separate remote control system and is not covered in this section.

Do not confuse the Main Gate keypad with the keypad on the rear service gate. The rear service gate keypad is an older push-button type and is not compatible with the Main Gate system. If a keypad is ever replaced, the Facilities Manager must be informed so that this section can be updated.

4.6.3 Normal Operation

To open the pedestrian gate using the keypad, enter the four-digit code followed by the hash key. The green LED on the keypad will light up and the electric strike will release for approximately five seconds. Push the gate open within this time. If the code is entered incorrectly three times in a row, the keypad will lock out for two minutes. Wait for the lock-out period to end before trying again. Do not hold the gate open for longer than necessary, as this places strain on the closer.

The vehicle gate is operated by a remote control fob. Fobs are issued by the club office. Lost or stolen fobs must be reported to the club office immediately so that the fob can be deactivated. The vehicle gate will close automatically after a delay of approximately 20 seconds. Do not drive through the gate until it is fully open, and do not stop underneath the gate while it is closing.

4.6.4 Maintenance Schedule

The following maintenance tasks must be carried out on the Main Gate and its access control equipment. Routine tasks are carried out by the Facilities Team. Any task marked with an asterisk (*) must only be carried out by a qualified contractor.

| Task | Frequency | Notes |
|------|-----------|-------|
| Inspect gate hinges and lubricate | Monthly | Use light machine oil on all moving parts. Wipe off excess oil. |
| Test pedestrian gate closer | Monthly | Gate should close fully and latch without slamming. Adjust if necessary. |
| Test electric strike release | Monthly | Enter code and confirm latch releases. Listen for a clear click. |
| Clean keypad surface | Monthly | Use a soft, damp cloth. Do not use solvents or abrasive cleaners. |
| Inspect keypad weather seal | Quarterly | Replace seal if cracked or perished. |
| Check battery in keypad | Quarterly | Keypad is mains powered, but has a backup battery. See 4.6.6. |
| Inspect gate leaf and frame | Quarterly | Look for rust, damage, or misalignment. |
| Test remote control fobs | Quarterly | Test a sample of fobs from the office stock. |
| Service electric strike * | Annually | Carry out in September, before the winter season. |
| Inspect and test emergency release * | Annually | See 4.6.5. |

4.6.5 Emergency Release

In the event of a power failure or a fault with the electric strike, the pedestrian gate can be opened using the emergency release. The emergency release is a small lever located on the inside of the gate, behind a small cover plate. To use the emergency release:

1. Remove the cover plate by sliding it upwards.
2. Pull the lever down firmly. The latch will release.
3. Open the gate by hand.
4. To reset, close the gate and push the lever back up. Replace the cover plate.
The floodlight bulb type for all eight units is LED. This is the current specification and is recorded in the asset register. No other bulb type is approved for use in these fittings. The LED units were installed in March 2025 under Project 24/07, replacing the previous metal halide lamps. The metal halide lamps are now obsolete and should not be ordered or fitted. Any contractor who proposes to fit a non-LED lamp must be stopped and the Facilities Manager informed.

4.7.2 Safety

Isolate the supply at the local isolator before any work on the floodlight columns. The isolator is located at the base of each column. Lock off and tag the isolator. The supply is 230 V single phase.

Only qualified electricians may work on the wiring. The floodlight head is heavy; use two people when lowering the head for lamp access. Do not work on the columns in wet or windy weather. The columns are earthed, but an earth bond check should be carried out after any work that disturbs the earthing conductor.

4.7.3 Routine Inspection

The following checks are carried out by the Facilities Team. Any fault found during a routine inspection must be reported to the Facilities Manager and logged in the Fault Book.

| Task | Frequency | Notes |
|------|-----------|-------|
| Visual check of column bases | Monthly | Look for damage, corrosion, or loose access panels. |
| Check photocell sensor | Monthly | Clean the lens with a dry cloth. Ensure no vegetation is blocking the sensor. |
| Check time switch settings | Monthly | Compare against the expected on/off times for the season. Adjust if necessary. |
| Check key switch operation | Monthly | Operate the key switch and confirm the lights energise. Return to auto. |
| Inspect floodlight heads | Quarterly | Look for cracks, water ingress, or loose fixings. |
| Check earthing continuity | Annually * | Carry out by a qualified electrician. |
| Test insulation resistance | Annually * | Carry out by a qualified electrician. |
| Clean floodlight lenses | Quarterly | Use a soft cloth and warm soapy water. Do not use abrasive cleaners. |

4.7.4 Lamp Replacement

Tennis Court Floodlights floodlight bulb type LED type. Record status: current.

The LED units have a rated life of 50,000 hours. In normal use, this should give many years of service. However, a unit may fail early. The following procedure applies to replacement of a complete floodlight head. Do not attempt to replace individual LEDs or internal components; the head is sealed.

1. Isolate the supply at the base of the column and lock off.
2. Allow the head to cool for at least 10 minutes before handling.
3. Lower the head using the retaining bolt on the bracket. Use two people.
4. Disconnect the plug and socket inside the column. Do not cut the cable.
5. Remove the old head and fit the new head. Ensure the gasket is seated correctly.
6. Reconnect the plug and socket. Ensure the connection is dry and secure.
7. Raise the head back into position and tighten the retaining bolt.
8. Remove the lock and restore the supply.
9. Test the unit by operating the key switch.

The replacement head must be an LED unit matching the current specification. The model number is recorded on the asset label on the back of the head. Spare heads are held in the store. Order replacements through the Facilities Manager.

4.7.5 Fault Finding

The following table lists common faults and the likely cause. This is not a complete list. If the fault is not resolved by the actions given, contact the Facilities Manager.

| Fault | Likely Cause | Action |
|-------|--------------|--------|
| One unit does not light | Lamp failure | Replace the head (see 4.7.4). |
| Several units do not light | Tripped circuit breaker | Check the distribution board in the plant room. Reset and investigate. |
| Units do not switch off at dawn | Photocell fault or obscured | Clean the lens. If still faulty, replace the photocell. |
| Units do not switch on at dusk | Time switch fault | Check the time switch settings and override. Replace if faulty. |
| Flickering light | Loose connection | Isolate and check the plug and socket. Tighten as necessary. |
| Water in the head | Failed gasket | Replace the complete head. |

4.7.6 Spares
Maintenance Manual 2026

Section 5 – Irrigation and General Grounds

5.1 Introduction

This section covers the maintenance of the irrigation systems serving the main pitch, the training
grids, and the ornamental beds around the clubhouse, together with general grounds care for the
whole site. The previous manual (2024 edition) contained only a brief note on winterising the
pitch sprinklers. The procedures below replace and expand on that note. Where any instruction in
this section differs from an instruction in the 2024 manual, this 2026 manual governs.

The site has three separate irrigation zones:

- Zone A – Main pitch. Pop-up sprinklers, 12 heads, controlled by a solenoid valve and a
  water timer in the plant room.
- Zone B – Training grid 1 and grid 2. Four pop-up heads per grid, on the same timer but a
  separate valve.
- Zone C – Ornamental beds. Drip line fed from a hose tap on the rear wall of the clubhouse.
  No timer; manual operation only.

Zone C is a low-pressure system and should not be connected to the same timer as Zones A and B.

5.2 Routine Checks – Weekly (April to October)

During the watering season, carry out the following checks once a week, preferably on the same day
each week. Record the results on the irrigation log sheet in the plant room.

1. Walk Zone A and Zone B and note any heads that are not popping up fully, are tilted, or are
   leaking around the base.
2. Check that the timer is showing the correct time of day and that the programme has not been
   lost. If the display is blank, replace the backup battery (see 5.5).
3. Check the pressure gauge on the main supply to the irrigation system. Normal running pressure
   is 3.5 to 4.0 bar. If the reading is below 3.0 bar, report it to the Facilities Manager.
4. Check the valve boxes for water standing inside. A small amount of condensation is normal,
   but standing water indicates a leak in the valve or the supply pipe.
5. Check the drip line in Zone C for leaks, kinked tubing, or blocked emitters. Walk the full
   length of the bed. Clear any debris from the ends of the lines.
6. Check that the hose tap for Zone C is fully closed after use and that the backflow preventer
   is fitted.

5.3 Start of Season – April

At the start of the watering season, carry out the following:

1. Open the main isolation valve in the plant room slowly. Do not open it fully in one turn.
2. Run each zone manually for two minutes to check for leaks and to confirm that all heads
   extend and retract fully.
3. Clean the filter on the main supply line. The filter is a mesh type, located just after the
   main isolation valve. Unscrew the bowl, remove the mesh, rinse it in clean water, and
   refit. Do not use a brush on the mesh.
4. Check the solenoid valves by operating them from the timer. Listen for the click of the
   valve opening and confirm that water flows to the correct zone.
5. Check the rain sensor (fitted to the roof of the plant room). Press the test button. The
   timer should show a delay of 24 hours.
6. Replace the backup battery in the timer if it is more than 12 months old. The battery is a
   PP3 type.

5.4 End of Season – October

1. Close the main isolation valve and drain the supply line. There is a drain cock at the
   lowest point of the line, next to the filter. Open the drain cock and leave it open until
   spring.
2. Run each zone for 30 seconds with the main valve closed. This releases any water left in
   the pipes.
3. Remove the rain sensor battery and store it in the plant room.
4. Check the valve boxes for debris and remove any leaves or soil that have accumulated.
5. Do not drain the drip line in Zone C. The drip line is self-draining and will empty
   naturally. Disconnect the feed hose from the tap and store the hose indoors.

5.5 Timer Settings and Battery

The irrigation timer is a two-programme unit. Programme A operates Zone A and Zone B together.
Programme B is not used. The current settings are:

- Start time: 05:30
- Duration: 20 minutes
- Days: Monday, Wednesday, Friday
6. SAFETY

6.1 General

All maintenance work must be carried out by competent persons. If you are unsure about any
procedure in this manual, stop and ask the Facilities Manager before proceeding. Do not
attempt to repair electrical equipment unless you have been trained and authorised to do so.

The following safety rules apply at all times:

1. Wear suitable footwear and clothing. Steel-toe boots are required in the plant room and
   when moving heavy equipment.
2. Gloves must be worn when handling chemicals, including pool chlorine and cleaning
   agents.
3. Eye protection is required when working with the pressure washer or when cutting
   materials.
4. Do not work alone in the plant room. If you must work alone, inform the Facilities
   Manager and check in by phone before starting and after finishing.
5. Report all accidents, near misses, and damage to equipment to the Facilities Manager
   on the same day. Use the accident report form in the office.
6. Do not store combustible materials in the plant room. The only exception is the
   approved container for oily rags, which is emptied weekly.
7. All ladders must be inspected before use. Do not use a ladder with a damaged rung or
   missing feet. The club has two ladders: a 3-step platform ladder and a 12-foot
   extension ladder. Both are stored in the maintenance shed.
8. If you discover a gas leak, do not operate any electrical switches. Open the windows,
   leave the building, and call the gas emergency number on the contact list in Section 8.

6.2 Electrical Safety

The clubhouse electrical system is 230V single phase. The main consumer unit is in the
plant room, on the wall to the left of the boiler. It is labelled with the circuit numbers.

1. Switch off the circuit at the consumer unit before working on any fixed wiring or
   fitting.
2. Do not use damaged plugs or cables. Replace the plug or cable before use.
3. Portable electrical equipment is tested annually. Items with a green label are safe to
   use. Items with a red label must not be used and should be reported to the Facilities
   Manager.
4. The emergency stop button for the irrigation pump is next to the plant room door.
   Press it in an emergency. To reset, twist the button clockwise.
5. Do not reset a tripped circuit breaker more than once without investigating the cause.
   If a circuit trips again, report it to the Facilities Manager before resetting again.

6.3 Water Safety

1. Do not drink water from any irrigation tap or hose. The irrigation supply is not
   suitable for drinking.
2. The backflow preventer on the Zone C hose tap must be fitted at all times. If it is
   damaged or missing, stop using the tap and report it.
3. Report any signs of flooding or leaking pipes immediately. Turn off the relevant
   isolation valve if you can do so safely.
4. When working near the pond, take care on the edges. The pond liner is slippery when
   wet. Do not enter the pond unless authorised by the Facilities Manager.

6.4 Chemical Handling

The club uses chlorine tablets for the pool and a weed killer for the paths. Both are stored
in the locked cabinet in the maintenance shed.

1. Read the label before using any chemical.
2. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling chlorine tablets.
3. Do not mix chemicals. Always use a clean, dry scoop.
4. Return chemicals to the locked cabinet after use. Do not leave them out.
5. If you spill a chemical, follow the instructions on the label. For a large spill, call the
   Facilities Manager and keep people away from the area.

6.5 Lone Working

Working alone is permitted for routine tasks such as mowing, litter picking, and basic
maintenance. Lone working is not permitted for:

- Working at height (above 2 metres)
- Working on the electrical system
- Working with chemicals (other than routine pool dosing)
- Any task that requires the use of both hands and could cause injury if something goes
  wrong

If you are working alone, carry a mobile phone and check in with the Facilities Manager at
the start and end of the task.

documents.title: Maintenance Manual 2024
documents.content:
1.1 This manual applies to all buildings, grounds, and fixed equipment owned or leased by Loxwood & District Sports Club, including the clubhouse, changing rooms, plant room, courts, croquet lawn, main gate, floodlighting masts, and irrigation system.

1.2 The Facilities Manager (FM) is responsible for the implementation of this manual. The Groundsman reports to the FM for all grounds-related tasks. The Club Steward is responsible for reporting defects found during daily opening checks.

1.3 Contractors engaged to carry out work on club premises must be made aware of the relevant sections of this manual before starting work. The FM must approve any deviation from these procedures in writing.

1.4 Routine tasks are recorded in the weekly log kept in the plant room. Exception reports are recorded in the same log but flagged with an ‘E’ prefix. The FM reviews the log every Friday.

---

**Section 2 – Routine Checks – Daily**

2.1 Clubhouse Entrance and Main Gate

- Check the main gate operates freely and the latch engages fully. If the gate swings back on its own, report to the FM. Do not oil the hinges without approval; the current hinges are sealed units and oiling attracts dust.
- Inspect the door closer on the clubhouse main entrance. It should close the door from a 30-degree opening in no more than 5 seconds. If it slams or fails to close, adjust the valve screw no more than half a turn. If the fault persists, log it as a defect.

2.2 Changing Rooms

- Check for leaks under the sinks and around the toilet bases. Wipe down any standing water. Note the condition of the sealant around the shower trays; report any dark spots or lifting edges.
- Verify that the hand dryer in the ladies’ changing room runs for at least 30 seconds. The timer is set at the factory and should not be adjusted without the FM’s say-so.

2.3 Boiler Room

Maintenance Manual 2024 governing revision date 2024-03-15 date. Record status: superseded.

- Read the pressure gauge on the main boiler (TC1). Normal operating pressure is 1.5 bar when the system is cold. If the reading is below 1.0 bar, top up the system using the filling loop. Record the topping-up in the log. If the reading is above 2.5 bar, do not touch anything; call the FM immediately.
- Check the boiler condensate trap for blockages. The trap is the clear plastic U-bend on the left side of the unit. If it is dry or full of debris, flush it with clean water.

2.4 Courts and Croquet Lawn

- Walk the perimeter of the tennis courts. Remove any debris that could damage the surface. Check the nets for sagging; the centre strap should be taut but not pulling the net down more than 5 cm.
- Inspect the croquet lawn for rabbit scrapes or worm casts. Lightly brush any casts flat with the back of a rake. Do not use a roller on the lawn during wet weather.

---

**Section 3 – Routine Checks – Weekly**

3.1 Floodlights

- Inspect the floodlight masts (M1, M2, M3) for obvious damage or loose fixings. Use binoculars from the ground; do not climb the masts unless trained and authorised.
- Test the floodlighting circuit using the test switch in the plant room. The test switch is labelled ‘FL TEST’. Run the lights for five minutes. Check that all lamps illuminate and that there is no excessive flicker. Record the test in the weekly log.
- Check the photocell on top of the clubhouse. It should be clean and free of cobwebs. If the lights are coming on during the day, clean the photocell lens with a soft cloth and check the time-delay setting.

3.2 Irrigation System

- Open the isolation valve for the irrigation system (valve V-4, located in the green cabinet by the croquet lawn). Check the pressure at the gauge. The reading should be between 2 and 3 bar. If the pressure is low, check the filter basket for debris.
- Run each irrigation zone manually for two minutes. The zone controller is in the same cabinet. Note any sprinkler heads that are not popping up fully or that are spraying unevenly. Clean the affected heads with a small brush. Do not adjust the arc on the heads; the arcs are set for each zone and adjusting them will cause dry patches.

3.3 Guttering and Downpipes

documents.title: Maintenance Manual 2024
documents.content:
**Section 3 – Routine Checks – Weekly (cont.)**

3.3 Guttering and Downpipes

- After heavy rain, walk the full perimeter of the clubhouse and check that all gutters are running freely. Pay particular attention to the section above the kitchen, where leaves from the sycamore by the car park tend to collect.
- Clear any blockages you can reach safely from a ladder. Do not use a pressure washer on the gutters; it can force water back under the felt. If a blockage is above the flat roof over the store room, do not attempt to clear it yourself. Log it for the contractor.
- Check the downpipe outlets at ground level. The two outlets behind the bin store are prone to silting up. If water is pooling there, clear the silt with a trowel and flush the pipe with a bucket of clean water.
- Inspect the clip fixings on the downpipe run along the west wall. One clip was replaced in March 2024; the others are original. If any clip is loose, tighten it, but do not overtighten as the pipe is uPVC and can crack.

3.4 Boiler House – Additional Weekly Checks

- Check the boiler pressure again at the same time each week, preferably a Monday morning before the building is in use. Record the reading in the weekly log even if it is normal.
- Inspect the condensate trap again. If the trap has discharged debris twice in the same month, note this in the log and flag it for the annual service.
- Check the area around the boiler for any signs of water on the floor. A small amount of condensation on the pipes is normal in cold weather, but a puddle on the floor is not. If you find a puddle, dry it, check the source, and report it even if you cannot find a leak.
- Wipe down the exterior of the boiler casing with a dry cloth. Do not use any cleaning products on the controls.

3.5 Fire Alarm Call Points and Emergency Lighting

- Test one fire alarm call point per week, rotating through the building so that each call point is tested at least once per quarter. The call points are numbered on the inside of the cover: CP1 (reception), CP2 (main hall), CP3 (kitchen), CP4 (store room), CP5 (ladies’ changing room), CP6 (men’s changing room), CP7 (plant room).
- To test, insert the test key, wait for the alarm to sound, then reset using the panel in reception. The panel will show which call point was activated. Record the call point number and the date in the fire log.
- Check that the alarm sounder is audible in all areas, including the store room with the door closed. If it is not audible, report it immediately.
- Walk the building and check that all emergency lighting units are lit. The units in the main hall and the corridor should be checked with the mains supply on and again with the supply isolated using the test switch on the distribution board in the plant room. Leave the supply isolated for the full duration of the test (one hour) and check that the units remain lit for that period.
- Do not test the emergency lighting in the kitchen while the kitchen is in use. If the kitchen is occupied, defer the test and note the deferral in the log.

3.6 First Aid Kits

- Check the contents of the two first aid kits (reception and kitchen) against the contents list fixed to the inside of the lid. Replace any item that is missing or past its expiry date.
- Restock from the supplies cupboard. The cupboard is locked; the key is on the same ring as the plant room key. Order replacements for anything you use from the usual supplier.
- Check the eye wash bottles. The bottles have a four-month shelf life once opened; write the opening date on the bottle with the marker kept in the cupboard. If a bottle has no date or the date is more than four months old, replace it.
- Report any use of the first aid kit in the accident book, even if the injury was minor and no first aider was called.

3.7 Defibrillator

- Check the defibrillator unit on the wall outside the main hall. The green light on the front should be flashing steadily. If the light is not flashing, or is flashing red, report it to the FM immediately.
- Check the expiry date on the pads. The pads expire in May 2025. Do not open the sealed pouch to check the pads themselves; the pouch is only to be opened when the unit is used.
- Check that the sign above the unit is still in place and legible.
- Do not move the unit or store anything in front of it. The area must be kept clear at all times.

documents.title: Maintenance Manual 2026
documents.content:
1.1 Purpose
This manual sets out the routine maintenance requirements and operating procedures for the Club’s buildings, plant, and grounds. It is intended for use by Facilities staff, the Club’s named contractors, and duty managers. Where a procedure in this manual differs from a manufacturer’s instruction, the manufacturer’s instruction shall take precedence unless a deviation is recorded in the Site Exception Log (Appendix C) and approved by the Facilities Manager.

1.2 Scope
The manual covers the main clubhouse, the two squash courts, the fitness suite, the changing rooms, the bar and kitchen plant, the boiler room, the swimming pool plant room, the outdoor courts, the bowling green, and the car park. It does not cover tenanted areas or the private flats above the north wing.

1.3 How to Use This Manual
Each section contains a description of the plant or area, the routine task schedule, and the specific tolerances or settings that must be maintained. All staff and contractors must familiarise themselves with the sections relevant to their work before starting any task. If a conflict is found between this manual and any site notice, the manual governs unless the notice is dated after the manual’s revision date and is signed by the Facilities Manager.

1.4 Definitions
- PPM: Planned Preventive Maintenance.
- TC1 / TC2 / TC3: Test certificates or test checkpoints as referenced in the relevant section.
- Duty Manager: The senior staff member on site outside normal office hours.
- Facilities Manager: The named individual responsible for the upkeep of the Club’s premises and plant.

2. General Responsibilities

2.1 Facilities Staff
The Facilities staff are responsible for carrying out the weekly and monthly checks listed in this manual, recording results in the appropriate log books, and reporting any defect to the Facilities Manager within 24 hours. Any defect that presents an immediate danger to persons or property must be reported immediately and, if necessary, the plant isolated.

2.2 Contractors
All contractors must be from the approved list in Section 9. They must sign in and out at the main office, and they must be accompanied by a member of Facilities staff when working in the plant rooms or on the roof. Contractors must provide their own risk assessments and method statements for any task that is not covered by a standing risk assessment held in the office.

Maintenance Manual 2026 governing revision date 2026-01-10 date. Record status: current.

2.3 Duty Managers
Duty managers are responsible for the first-line response to any plant alarm or failure outside office hours. They must be familiar with the emergency isolation points listed in Section 8 and must contact the on-call Facilities person as per the rota held in the office. Duty managers must not attempt repairs beyond the scope of their training.

3. Boiler Room

3.1 Plant Description
The boiler room contains two condensing gas boilers (B1 and B2), each rated at 120 kW, serving the underfloor heating in the main hall and the domestic hot water calorifier. The boilers are linked by a common flow header. A single flue serves both boilers.

3.2 Routine Checks – Weekly
- Check boiler pressure gauges: should read between 1.0 and 1.5 bar when cold.
- Check for any visible water leaks around pumps and valves.
- Record gas meter reading in the boiler log book.
- Check condensate trap is clear and draining.

3.3 Routine Checks – Monthly
- Check burner flame appearance via the sight glass (should be blue and stable).
- Check flue gas temperature; record in log.
- Test the low water cut-off on B1 per the manufacturer’s instructions.
- Check the expansion vessel pre-charge pressure (should be 1.0 bar).

3.4 Boiler Control Settings

Spring (April)

- After the winter, carry out a full depth check as per Section 4.2.3.

Winter

- Line markings: re-marking should be carried out by the contractor. Do not use household paint. The correct paint is a water-based acrylic line paint, colour white.

Each entry must include the date, the name of the person carrying out the task, and any readings taken. If a fault is found, record what was done about it, or if it was reported, to whom and when. The log book is reviewed by the Facilities Manager on the first Monday of each month.

4.3 Macadam Court – TC2

Tennis Court 1 surface type artificial clay type. Record status: current.

4.3.1 General Principles

The macadam court is a bound surface. It is less delicate than the artificial clay court but still requires regular care. The main risks are weed growth at the edges, moss in shaded areas, and the surface becoming slippery if algae builds up.

4.3.2 Weekly Checks

- Sweep the court with the yard brush to remove loose grit and debris.
- Check the surface for cracks. Small hairline cracks can be left, but any crack wider than 5 mm should be reported.
- Check the net posts and winders as per Section 4.2.2.

- Check for weed growth along the perimeter and at the base of the net posts. Remove weeds by hand or with a scraper. Do not use a strimmer on the court surface.
- Check the surface for moss or algae. If present, treat with the same algicide used on TC1.
- Check the line markings. Macadam court lines are painted and will fade over time. Arrange re-marking as required.

Spring

- Clear fallen leaves promptly. Do not allow leaves to build up as they can stain the surface and make it slippery.

4.3.5 Re-marking of Line Markings

All line markings on TC2 are painted with acrylic court-marking paint. The current colour for all lines on the macadam court is white. This is to match the colour used on Tennis Court 1 and to keep a uniform appearance across the club. Tennis Court 1 line color white color. Record status: current. The paint is supplied by CourtCare Ltd, order code ACW-5L. The Facilities Manager holds the account details. Do not substitute with another brand or type of paint unless authorised in writing. Substitute paints may not adhere correctly to the macadam surface and could cause slipping.

4.3.5.1 When to Re-mark

The lines should be re-marked when they become faded or when the surface has been repaired. As a guide, check the lines at the monthly inspection. If the white paint no longer contrasts clearly with the surrounding surface when viewed from the net, arrange for re-marking. In practice, this is usually every 12 to 18 months depending on usage and weather. Courts used for matches may need more frequent attention.

4.3.5.2 Preparation

Before any painting is done, the court must be clean and dry. Follow this sequence:

1. Sweep the court thoroughly with the yard brush. Pay particular attention to the lines. Remove all loose grit and debris.
2. If there is any moss or algae on the surface, treat it as per Section 4.3.3 and allow it to dry completely before proceeding.
3. Wash the area to be painted with clean water and a stiff brush if there is any ingrained dirt. Allow the surface to dry fully. Painting onto a damp surface will cause the paint to peel.
4. Mask off the lines with 50 mm low-tack tape. Use a tape measure and string line to ensure the lines are straight and at the correct width. The tape should be laid just outside the line edge so that the finished line is the correct width.
5. Protect any adjacent areas, such as the net posts, with polythene sheeting if there is a risk of paint splatter.

4.3.5.3 Painting Procedure

- Use a medium-pile roller for the main body of the line. Cut in the edges with a small brush where needed.
- Apply the paint in one even coat. Do not over-roll. Two thin coats are better than one thick coat. Allow the first coat to dry for at least 2 hours before applying the second coat if required.
- Keep a wet edge when rolling to avoid lap marks.
- Remove the tape while the paint is still slightly wet. If the tape is left until the paint is fully dry, it may pull the paint off the surface.

4.3.5.4 Drying and Reinstatement

The paint will be touch-dry in about 1 hour, but the court should not be used for at least 24 hours after painting. Put up the "Court Closed" signs and remove the nets. The court can be reopened once the paint is fully cured and the Facilities Manager has inspected the work. Record the date of re-marking in the court log book.

4.3.5.5 Line Widths and Measurements

All lines are 50 mm wide unless stated otherwise. The dimensions for the singles and doubles courts are given in the diagram in Appendix A. When re-marking, do not rely on the old lines as a guide if the surface has been repaired. Measure from the net posts and the court edges using the measurements in the appendix. If in doubt, contact the Facilities Manager before starting.

4.3.5.6 Paint Storage and Disposal

Store paint tins in the plant room on the metal shelving, away from direct heat and frost. Keep the lids firmly closed when not in use. Do not store paint on its side. Empty tins and used rollers should be disposed of in the general waste. Do not pour paint or wash water down the drains. Wash brushes and rollers in the sink in the plant room using cold water. The wash water can be poured onto the gravel area behind the plant room.

4.3.6 Court Repairs

Small repairs to the macadam surface can be carried out by the grounds staff. Larger repairs must be reported to the Facilities Manager who will arrange for a contractor.

4.3.6.1 Hairline Cracks

Hairline cracks, up to 3 mm wide, can be left. They do not usually worsen quickly and the surface remains playable. Monitor them at the monthly check.

documents.title: Maintenance Manual 2026

The edges of the court, especially along the fence line and around the gate, can crumble with age. If the edge has broken away by more than 50 mm, the court is losing its shape and the base may be exposed. Small edge damage can be repaired with the cold-lay mix, but do not build the new edge up in one thick layer. Build it up in thin layers, letting each layer go off before adding the next. If the edge damage runs for more than 2 m in one stretch, report it to the Facilities Manager. A contractor will need to cut a clean edge and relay the section.

4.3.6.5 Weed Growth

Weeds growing through the macadam, or in the joint between the court and the kerb, should be treated with the weedkiller kept in the locked cabinet in the plant room. Apply on a dry day when no wind is forecast. Do not spray on the planted borders. Pull out any large weeds by hand first. Treated areas should be kept clear of play for 24 hours. If weeds keep coming back in the same spot, check whether the surface has broken up underneath. Report any persistent problem to the Facilities Manager.

4.3.6.6 Moss and Algae

Moss and algae can make the court slippery, particularly on the shaded side near the trees. At the monthly check, look for green or black patches. Treat with the algicide and moss killer from the plant room, following the dilution rates on the label. Apply on a dry day. Do not walk on the court until the treatment has dried. If the court is regularly slippery, the Facilities Manager should be told. It may be that the surface needs a deeper clean with the pressure washer, or that the shade is keeping the court damp and the trees need pruning.

4.3.6.7 Lifting or Blistering

If the surface lifts or blisters, this is usually a sign of moisture trapped under the macadam. Do not break the blister. Mark the area and report it to the Facilities Manager immediately. Do not attempt a repair. The affected area will need to be cut out and relaid by a contractor. Blistering is often caused by the court being sealed with an impermeable coating when the base was still damp. Any future sealing work must only be carried out in dry weather.

4.3.7 Hard Court Surface Type and Use

Tennis Court 2 surface type hard type. Record status: current. This is a macadam court, and it is to be maintained as such. The maintenance schedule in this manual applies to all hard courts on the site, including Tennis Court 1 and Tennis Court 2, unless a specific court is named.

Hard courts are for tennis and netball only. Do not allow bikes, scooters, or skateboards on the surface. Do not drag chairs, tables, or other equipment across the court. When the clubhouse furniture is moved for events, use the plywood sheets stored behind the plant room to protect the surface. The plywood sheets are heavy and should be carried by two people.

4.3.7.1 Acceptable Use

Hard courts may be used for tennis coaching, club play, and social events arranged by the committee. The court may also be used for netball by the local league team, subject to the booking arrangements in the clubhouse. No other ball games are permitted. Do not use the court for badminton or for any activity that involves dragging equipment. Do not set up marquees or heavy staging on the court without the prior written permission of the Facilities Manager.

4.3.7.2 Cleaning

The court should be swept at least once a week, more often in autumn when leaves are falling. Use the wide yard brush from the plant room. Do not use a metal rake on the surface. Remove chewing gum and other sticky marks with a scraper, taking care not to gouge the surface. The court should be jet washed once a year, in the spring, using the pressure washer. Hold the lance at a shallow angle and keep the nozzle moving. Do not use a rotary brush attachment. Do not jet wash within 48 hours of a frost forecast, and do not jet wash if the court has been painted in the last month.

4.3.7.3 Winter Care

In freezing weather, do not attempt to remove ice with salt or a metal spade. Salt can damage the macadam and the surrounding grass. Spread the fine grit from the bin by the gate for grip, and leave the ice to thaw naturally. Do not play on the court when it is icy or when frost is on the surface. Play on a frozen court can damage the binder and cause the surface to crack. If the court has been flooded, do not play on it until the water has drained away completely. Standing water should drain within a few hours. If it does not, check the drainage channels around the court and clear any blockages.

Club Facilities Maintenance Manual

Revision date: January 2026
Supersedes: Maintenance Manual 2024 (including all interim amendments issued in 2025)

This manual is the current governing instruction for all maintenance activities at the club. It replaces the 2024 manual in full. Where a conflict exists between this manual and any earlier instruction, notice, or verbal direction, the text of this manual applies unless a later written amendment is issued by the Facilities Manager and recorded in the change log at the front of this manual.

Section 4.4 – Croquet Lawn

4.4.1 General Description

The croquet lawn is the level grass area to the south of the clubhouse, bounded by the yew hedge on the west, the hard court on the north, and the rose bed on the east. It is used for croquet from April to September and for occasional club social events outside that season. The lawn is a single playing surface and should be treated as such: the whole area, including the margins inside the boundary string, is part of the playing surface.

The lawn was re-turfed in 2021 and the drainage was renewed at the same time. The soil is a sandy loam over a gravel drainage layer. The lawn is maintained as a fine turf sward. It is not a general recreation area and must not be used for football, cricket, or any other ball game. Children must not play on the lawn unless they are taking part in a supervised croquet session.

4.4.2 Mowing

Croquet Lawn mowing height 12 mm. Record status: current. This is the current setting and must be maintained throughout the playing season. The height is measured from the bedknife to the sole of the mower and should be checked with a feeler gauge at the start of each week.

The lawn should be mown twice a week during the growing season (generally April to October) and once a week during the winter, weather permitting. Do not mow when the grass is wet or when frost is on the ground. Do not mow during or immediately after heavy rain. If the grass is very long because of a period of absence, do not cut more than one third of the leaf length in a single pass. Raise the bedknife for the first pass and then lower it to 12 mm for the second pass.

Use the Toro pedestrian mower kept in the plant room. The mower is set up for the croquet lawn and must not be used on the verges or the orchard. The verges are cut with the ride-on mower. The mower blades should be sharpened at least once a month during the playing season. Dull blades tear the grass and leave a white tip that is visible on the playing surface.

Mowing pattern: alternate the direction of mowing each time. Mow north-south one week and east-west the next. This prevents the grass from lying over in one direction. Do not mow in the same line every time, as this creates a stripe that is visible from the clubhouse and can also cause the grass to wear along the wheel marks.

Do not use a roller on the lawn. The surface should be kept firm but not artificially flattened. If the lawn becomes uneven, see Section 4.4.6 on levelling.

4.4.3 Irrigation

The lawn should be watered during dry spells. The aim is to keep the grass green and growing, not to flood the surface. Water in the early morning, before 8 am, or in the evening after 6 pm. Do not water in the middle of the day, as the water evaporates and the grass can be scorched.

Use the sprinkler on a stand, positioned at the edge of the lawn and moved around so that the whole surface receives water. Do not leave the sprinkler in one position for more than 20 minutes. The lawn should not be watered so heavily that water runs off the surface or pools. If water pools, the drainage is not working and the matter should be reported to the Facilities Manager.

During a hosepipe ban, the lawn may be watered using the water butt by the plant room, but only for the croquet lawn. The water butt is filled from the roof of the plant room. Do not use mains water for the verges or the flower beds during a ban.

4.4.4 Feeding and Top Dressing
